title: Coco Coir Properties and Management
objective: Explain coir's physical and exchange properties and build a batch-specific management plan for salts, calcium, magnesium, and potassium.

terms.definition: Fine material from coconut husk processing, also called coco peat or dust.
Longer coir particles that increase structure and larger pores.
Coarse husk particle used to increase aeration and structural persistence.
Commercial treatment intended to alter exchange-site occupancy; not the same as simple rinsing.

coreScience: Coir products are made from coconut husks and may contain pith, fiber, chips, or blends. Particle distribution controls water retention and aeration. Coir is generally easier to rewet than dry peat, but air-water behavior still depends on processing, compaction, container, and irrigation.

Coir can contain substantial potassium, sodium, and chloride if processing and washing are inadequate. Its exchange sites interact with calcium, magnesium, potassium, and sodium. 'Buffered' is a processing claim that should be supported by supplier quality data and incoming pH/EC or laboratory testing.

A cannabis pot study comparing peat, a peat/green-fiber blend, and coir in two genotypes found substrate- and genotype-dependent effects on biomass, roots, floral yield, and cannabinoid measures. It is evidence that substrate matters, not proof that one category wins in every system.

cultivationRelevance: Hydrate compressed blocks with measured water, account for expansion, mix completely, and sample the finished lot rather than only the runoff from the first container.

Develop irrigation and nutrition from measured root-zone behavior. Coir's frequent-irrigation reputation does not mean roots should remain continuously saturated or that runoff targets can be copied blindly.

measureAndRecord.requirement: Source, grade, pith/fiber/chip blend, lot, declared wash/buffer process.
Expansion ratio, moisture, pH, EC, Na, Cl, K, Ca, and Mg when tested.
Hydration water, volume, rinse or conditioning action, and mixing.
Input and root-zone pH/EC, irrigation frequency, runoff method, and roots.
Tissue Ca/Mg/K, growth, symptoms, yield, and chemistry with genotype.

misconceptions: Coco is inert: It has organic structure and meaningful exchange behavior.
Rinsing and buffering are identical: Rinsing removes soluble salts; buffering changes exchange-site occupancy under a defined treatment.
Coco requires one universal calcium-magnesium supplement: Need depends on water, base fertilizer, processing, exchange status, and tissue response.
evidenceLimits: Coir varies strongly by source and processing. Extract values depend on method, and responses from two study genotypes do not establish universal cannabis targets.
